IBD & Endocrinopathies

Gut disease that shows in the mouth — coeliac disease, ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s disease and orofacial granulomatosis — then the endocrine system and diabetes mellitus, from insulin physiology to the hypoglycaemic patient in your chair.

Dr Joseph Ryan

01

The mouth as a window on the gut

Why these patients are complex, the oral clues, and the medical work-up.

Patient safety

Patients are complex, often with many conditions; they may have limited knowledge of their own medical history; poor collaboration between medical disciplines can lead to poor outcomes. Hence the need for familiarity with common conditions.

Learning outcomes

  • Working knowledge of causes, clinical features and management of common GI diseases
  • Detailed knowledge of their oral manifestations
  • Knowledge and skills to provide dental treatment to these patients
Oral signExample GI / systemic cause
Mouth ulcersCrohn’s disease
Dental erosionGORD, eating disorders
BleedingNutritional deficiency, cirrhosis
HalitosisFetor hepaticus (the musty breath of liver failure)
CandidaMedication side effect
HyposalivationAmphetamine

The medical work-up

History and examinationBloods: FBC, UEC, LFT, lipaseImaging: CT, X-ray, MRIScopesPill cameraBiopsyBariumTrial treatment

FBC = full blood count; UEC = urea, electrolytes, creatinine (kidney function); LFT = liver function tests; lipase = pancreatic enzyme.

02

Coeliac disease

Gluten-driven small-bowel inflammation — with a dental fingerprint.

Definition

A small bowel disorder characterised by mucosal inflammation, villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia, which occur on exposure to dietary gluten and improve after withdrawal of gluten from the diet.

1–1.5% of the communityFamilial clusteringLow risk: Chinese, Japanese, Sub-Saharan African descent

GI symptoms: chronic or recurrent diarrhoea or constipation, malabsorption, unexpected weight loss, abdominal pain, distension, bloating.

Why the villi flatten (textbook context)

Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten (gliadin) in people carrying HLA-DQ2 or DQ8. Tissue transglutaminase modifies gliadin, which then drives a T-cell response that damages enterocytes. Loss of villi = loss of absorptive surface → malabsorption of iron, folate and B12 — and that is the source of many of the oral signs. Screening uses coeliac antibodies (tTG-IgA), done while the patient is still eating gluten.

Oral signs

Teeth

Dental enamel defects

The most specific oral sign — typically symmetrical and in the same tooth groups, reflecting disease while the enamel formed in childhood.

Mucosa

RAS-like ulceration

Aphthous-like ulcers, likely secondary to anaemia (haematinic deficiency).

Tongue

Atrophic glossitis, glossodynia

Smooth, sore tongue — again from iron, folate or B12 deficiency.

Treatment

Elimination of gluten from the diet. Oral ulceration and glossitis improve as the haematinics recover; established enamel defects do not.

Which oral sign is most strongly associated with coeliac disease: cobblestone mucosa, enamel defects, pyostomatitis vegetans or fetor hepaticus?

Dental enamel defects. Cobblestone mucosa points to Crohn’s disease or OFG, pyostomatitis vegetans to IBD (especially UC), and fetor hepaticus to liver failure.

03

Inflammatory bowel disease: overview

An idiopathic, relapsing, life-long inflammation of the gut.

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)

Idiopathic, life-long, relapsing and remitting inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract — the two main forms are Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC).

Gut

Intestinal symptoms

Abdominal pain; diarrhoea with blood and mucus; tiredness; weight loss; fever; nausea and vomiting.

Beyond the gut

Extra-intestinal

Oral mucosal ulceration; pain and swelling around the anus; swollen joints; inflamed eyes; cutaneous rash or lumps; jaundice.

Australian epidemiology

Among the highest reported incidence worldwide75,000 Australians living with IBD~1622 new cases / year~50:50 CD:UCTypical onset 15–40 ySlight female predominance in CDLower in Asia and the Middle East
How old is that number?

The figures are from Wilson et al. (2010). Prevalence has kept rising; more recent Australian estimates put the number living with IBD at well over 100,000. Quote the lecture figure in the exam, but know it is a 2010 snapshot.

From the lecture slides
04

Crohn’s disease vs ulcerative colitis

The comparison table you must be able to reproduce.

FeatureCrohn’s diseaseUlcerative colitis
SiteAnywhere, mouth to anusColon only
PatternDiscontinuous (skip lesions)Continuous, retrograde, beginning at the rectum
InflammationTransmural; granulomas may be presentMucosal; no granulomas
Extracolonic diseaseAbscesses, fistulae, perianal fistulasNo
One word for each

Crohn’s = “cobblestones, skips and fistulas” (patchy, deep, granulomatous). UC = “continuous from the rectum, mucosa only”. The rectum is almost always involved in UC and is often spared in CD.

Describe the difference in inflammatory pattern between Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.

Crohn’s disease is discontinuous (skip lesions with normal bowel between), can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, and is transmural — involving the full thickness of the wall, often with non-caseating granulomas, which allows fissures, fistulae, abscesses and fibrotic strictures. Ulcerative colitis is continuous, starts at the rectum and spreads proximally, is confined to the colon, and is mucosal with no granulomas, so fistulae do not form.

Which feature distinguishes ulcerative colitis from Crohn’s disease: transmural inflammation, skip lesions, involvement of the rectum, or granulomas?

Involvement of the rectum. UC always starts in the rectum and extends continuously. The other three options are all features of Crohn’s disease.

05

Ulcerative colitis: oral features and management

Pyostomatitis vegetans and friends.

Specific

Pyostomatitis vegetans

Multiple yellow pustules on red, thickened mucosa with a “snail-track” appearance as they rupture. A marker of IBD, most often UC.

Skin/mucosa

Pyoderma gangrenosum

Necrotic, rapidly enlarging ulceration — a neutrophilic dermatosis associated with IBD.

Common

Aphthous ulceration

Recurrent minor aphthae, often tracking disease activity.

Common

Halitosis

Listed on the slide as an oral feature.

Management

  1. Reduce inflammation
    Sulfasalazine — anti-inflammatory action on intestinal tissue (a 5-aminosalicylate prodrug).
  2. Corticosteroids in non-responders
    For flares not controlled by 5-ASA.
  3. Steroid-sparing drugs
    To avoid the harms of long-term steroids.
The oral take-home

Treating the systemic disease normally resolves the aphthae. Refractory lesions are treated the same way as ordinary recurrent aphthous ulceration.

From the lecture slides
06

Crohn’s disease and its oral manifestations

A panenteric disease that can announce itself in the mouth.

Crohn’s disease

First reported in 1932 by Crohn. A panenteric disease that can affect every part of the GI tract from mouth to anus (small and large intestine most common). Features non-caseating granulomas, transmural inflammation and skip lesions; can cause fibrosis and obstruction.

Aetiopathogenesis — and the L3B link

Idiopathic. Current theory: gut bacteria, in a genetically susceptible host, trigger an inappropriate immune reaction → chronic inflammation and ulceration. The non-caseating granulomas are the granulomatous chronic inflammation of L3B — activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) and giant cells, without the caseous necrosis of TB.

Oral manifestations

9–50% of patientsMay precede intestinal symptoms in 60% of those with oral involvement
FeatureWhat you see
Aphthous-like ulcerationCommon, non-specific
Linear ulcerationDeep ulcers in the buccal sulcus/vestibule, often with hyperplastic folds
CobblestoningInflammatory hyperplasia of the oral mucosa in a cobblestone pattern
Mucosal tags / polypoid lesionsIndurated polypoid lesions in the vestibule and retromolar pad
Facial and lip swellingDiffuse, persistent
GingivitisRed, swollen gingiva extending to the mucosal transition
Pyostomatitis vegetansAlso seen in CD
Which oral manifestation of Crohn’s disease can precede the gastrointestinal symptoms?

Of the tutorial options, pyostomatitis vegetans. More generally, oral lesions (cobblestoning, linear ulcers, mucosal tags, lip swelling) precede intestinal symptoms in about 60% of patients who have oral involvement — so the dentist may be first to suspect the diagnosis.

From the lecture slides
07

Investigating and managing IBD

From primary-care screening to biologics.

Primary care

Screening (with the clinical picture)

  • Full blood examination (anaemia)
  • Urea and electrolytes
  • Iron studies, B12, folate
  • CRP, ESR (inflammation)
  • Coeliac antibodies (exclude coeliac)
  • Stool: faecal calprotectin — a neutrophil-derived protein
Specialist

Diagnosis

  • Serology: ASCA (anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody) and atypical p-ANCA
  • Endoscopy and tissue biopsy (the definitive test)
  • Capsule endoscopy (Pill-Cam) for the small bowel
  • Imaging: radiographs incl. CT, ultrasound
Reading the serology (textbook context)

ASCA-positive, p-ANCA-negative favours Crohn’s; p-ANCA-positive, ASCA-negative favours UC. Neither is diagnostic alone. Faecal calprotectin rises when neutrophils pour into the bowel lumen, so it separates inflammatory disease (IBD) from functional bowel disease (IBS).

Medical management

GroupExamples
5-aminosalicylates (5-ASA)Sulfasalazine, mesalamine
AntibioticsCiprofloxacin, metronidazole
Conventional corticosteroidsPrednisolone
Topical / intralesional corticosteroidsBudesonide
ImmunomodulatorsAzathioprine, methotrexate
BiologicsInfliximab, adalimumab (anti-TNF)
Continued resistant diseaseChronic low-dose steroids; total parenteral nutrition (TPN); surgery
Why the drug list matters to a dentist

Steroids → adrenal suppression and poor healing; azathioprine, methotrexate and biologics → immunosuppression (infection, and long-term malignancy risk — see section 9); metronidazole → drug interactions. Anti-TNF drugs block the TNF of L3A, so the acute inflammatory response itself is blunted.

From the lecture slides
08

Orofacial granulomatosis (OFG)

Crohn’s-like granulomas confined to the face and mouth.

Definition

Term introduced by Wiesenfeld et al. (1985): granulomas in the orofacial region in the absence of any recognised systemic condition. It encompasses the previously recognised Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome and cheilitis granulomatosa of Miescher.

Melkersson–Rosenthal triad

(1) Persistent lip or facial swelling · (2) recurrent facial paralysis · (3) fissured tongue.

The slides spell these “Melkerssohn” and “Mieschke”; the standard spellings are Melkersson and Miescher.

Cause?

Aetiological controversies

Genetics · food allergy · allergy to dental materials · infective · immunological.

Presentation

Clinical picture

Variable. Most commonly the upper and/or lower lip, but also chin, cheeks, periorbital region and eyelids. May be unilateral. Episodic, becoming persistent; feel changes from soft to firm.

Other features

Cobblestoning of buccal mucosaAngular cheilitisMucosal ulcerationVertical fissures of the lipsMucosal tagsLingua plicata (fissured tongue)
“Sounds like oral Crohn’s, doesn’t it!”

The lecturer’s point: OFG and oral Crohn’s look the same clinically and histologically. OFG is a diagnosis of exclusion — you must actively look for Crohn’s, sarcoidosis and TB, and keep looking over time.

Diagnosis: rule out TB, Crohn’s and sarcoidosis

TestWhy
BiopsyDemonstrates granulomatous inflammation; negative special stains for organisms; no foreign material
Chest radiographHilar adenopathy → TB or sarcoidosis
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)Raised in sarcoidosis (but also in OFG)
Faecal calprotectinGut inflammation → Crohn’s
Folic acid, iron, B12Decreased in Crohn’s (malabsorption)
QuantiFERON-TB GoldBlood test for TB infection

Management

  1. Elimination diet
    Cinnamon- and benzoate-free diet.
  2. Topical therapy
    Topical steroid and tacrolimus ointment.
  3. Intralesional steroids
    Injected into the swollen lip.
  4. Systemic therapy
    Systemic steroids; steroid-sparing immunomodulators (clofazimine, dapsone); biologics (most trials have been in CD).
  5. Surgery
    Reduction cheiloplasty for persistent deformity.
Why is OFG described as a diagnosis of exclusion, and which three conditions must be excluded?

Because its granulomas are indistinguishable from those of systemic granulomatous diseases. By definition OFG is granulomatous inflammation without a recognised systemic cause, so Crohn’s disease, sarcoidosis and tuberculosis must be excluded (plus infection and foreign-body reaction on biopsy, using special stains and polarised light).

From the lecture slides
09

Dental care in Crohn’s patients

Gentleness, hygiene and the long tail of immunosuppression.

Approach

The patient

Benefit from gentleness and patience; they have had their share of doctors, procedures, needles and medications; oral care may not be a priority; oral lesions can make hygiene difficult.

Risk

Longitudinal immunosuppression

Increased risk of malignancy. The slide’s case: a 73-year-old woman with a T4 squamous cell carcinoma on long-term azathioprine for Crohn’s.

Link to L5C and L7

Iatrogenic immunosuppression is an acquired immunodeficiency (L5C). Reduced immune surveillance allows malignant clones to escape (L7) — so examine the oral mucosa carefully at every visit in patients on long-term immunosuppressants.

A 28-year-old woman has multiple oral ulcers, weight loss, diarrhoea and fatigue; there is cobblestone mucosa and linear vestibular ulceration. Diagnosis, a confirmatory blood test, and the impact on dental treatment?

Most likely diagnosis: Crohn’s disease with oral involvement (cobblestoning and linear ulcers are characteristic).

Blood test: ASCA serology supports Crohn’s (with FBE, iron studies/B12/folate and CRP/ESR to show anaemia and inflammation). Diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy and biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas; faecal calprotectin is the stool test.

Impact on dental care: liaise with the gastroenterologist; ask about steroids (adrenal suppression), immunosuppressants/biologics (infection risk, slower healing, mucosal malignancy surveillance); check for anaemia; manage painful lesions and support hygiene; be gentle and keep appointments short; avoid prescribing NSAIDs, which can trigger IBD flares.

10

The endocrine system

Hormones, feedback and the two ways a hormone talks to a cell.

Definitions

Clinical endocrinology: the branch of medicine dedicated to diseases of the endocrine glands, which secrete hormones into the bloodstream.
Hormone: a substance, usually a peptide or steroid, produced by one tissue and conveyed by the bloodstream to another to effect physiological activity — i.e. it can act on target cells distant from its site of synthesis.

Feedback inhibition

Increased activity of the target tissue often down-regulates the gland that secretes the stimulating hormone. Example: thyroid hormone (T3/T4) suppresses TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the pituitary. Most endocrine disease is either too much hormone, too little, or a broken feedback loop.

 Cell-surface receptor hormonesIntracellular receptor hormones
ExamplesPeptides (growth hormone, insulin) and small molecules (adrenaline)Lipid-soluble: steroids (glucocorticoids), retinoids (vitamin A), thyroxine
HowBind outside → signal transduction insideDiffuse across the membrane, bind receptors in cytosol or nucleus → complex binds promoter/enhancer DNA
EffectChanges proliferation, differentiation, survival and function, mainly by regulating gene productsDirectly alters gene transcription
From the lecture slides
11

The endocrine pancreas and glucose homeostasis

One per cent of the pancreas, and the hormones that run blood sugar.

Pancreas

Two organs in one

The exocrine pancreas makes digestive enzymes; the endocrine pancreas is only 1–2% of the gland: about 1 million islets of Langerhans. Its most significant disorders are diabetes mellitus and neoplasms.

Islet hormones

Three products

Insulin (β cells) · glucagon (α cells) · somatostatin (δ cells). (Cell names are textbook context.)

Why pancreatic disease is found late

The pancreas is retroperitoneal and its signs and symptoms are vague, so many pancreatic diseases progress undiagnosed for long periods.

Glucose homeostasis is set by three things

  1. Glucose production in the liver
    From stored glycogen and by making new glucose.
  2. Glucose uptake and use by peripheral tissues
    Mainly skeletal muscle.
  3. Insulin and counter-regulatory hormones
    e.g. glucagon.

What insulin does

Its principal metabolic function is to increase glucose transport into certain cells; overall its effects are anabolic — increased synthesis and reduced breakdown of glycogen, lipid and protein. It is also important for DNA synthesis, growth and differentiation of some cells. The most important stimulus for insulin release is glucose itself.

TissueInsulin’s actions (Robbins figure, slide 40)
Skeletal muscle↑ glucose uptake · ↑ glycogen synthesis · ↑ protein synthesis
Adipose tissue↑ glucose uptake · ↑ lipogenesis · ↓ lipolysis
Liver↓ gluconeogenesis · ↑ glycogen synthesis · ↑ lipogenesis
Where diabetes comes from

Abnormalities at any point along the signalling cascade — from insulin synthesis and release by β cells to receptor interactions in peripheral tissues — can give the diabetic phenotype.

From the lecture slides
12

Diabetes mellitus: type 1 vs type 2

One feature in common — hyperglycaemia — reached by two different routes.

Diabetes mellitus

A group of metabolic disorders sharing the common underlying feature of hyperglycaemia. Morbidity comes from macrovascular disease (atherosclerosis) and microvascular disease (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy).

 Type 1 (~10%)Type 2 (>90%)
MechanismInsulin deficiency from destruction of pancreatic β cellsHyperglycaemia with variable insulin deficiency and resistance
WhoOne of the commonest chronic diseases of childhood (~2/3 of DM in patients <19 y); incidence 0.1–37 / 100,000 children <15 yAdults (but increasingly children); US adult prevalence ~5–12%
CauseGenetic susceptibility + an environmental trigger that has never been definitively identifiedObesity, genetic susceptibility, behaviour (activity, diet, smoking, alcohol, weight, sleep)
Protective—Mediterranean diet (fruit, vegetables, nuts, whole grains, olive oil)
InsulinAlways needed (pump ± sensor)Often oral drugs first (metformin)
EmergencyDKADKA rare
Link to L5B

The β-cell destruction of type 1 is autoimmune: autoreactive T cells attack the islets, and autoantibodies (e.g. against insulin and GAD) appear years before diagnosis. It is a textbook organ-specific autoimmune disease.

From the lecture slides
13

Presentation, risk factors and diagnosis

Most patients have no symptoms; the classic triad, and how it is confirmed.

The key fact

The majority of patients are asymptomatic — hyperglycaemia is noted on routine blood tests, prompting further testing.

Symptom

Polydipsia

Thirst.

Symptom

Polyuria

Excess urination; nocturia.

Symptom

Blurred vision

Lens osmotic change.

Less frequent

Weight loss

Glucose exceeds the renal threshold and calories are lost in urine.

Incidental

Infection

May first present when a UTI or gastro unmasks it.

Why polyuria and thirst?

Once blood glucose rises above what the kidney can reabsorb, glucose spills into urine and pulls water with it (osmotic diuresis) → polyuria → dehydration → thirst.

Type 2 risk factors

ObesityPositive family historyNon-European ethnicity (Asian, ATSI)Female genderInsulin-resistance conditions (e.g. PCOS)

Confirmatory tests

If symptoms + very high fasting/random glucose, or two high fasting glucose readings:

  1. HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin)
    ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol). Reflects average glucose over the ~3-month life of a red cell.
  2. Oral glucose tolerance test
    Fasting blood test at 0 min → 75 g oral glucose → blood glucose at 2 h (sometimes 1 h).
Numbers worth knowing (Australian criteria, textbook context)

The slide gives HbA1c “>6.5%”; the formal cut-off is ≥ 6.5%. Glucose thresholds for diabetes: fasting ≥ 7.0 mmol/L; random or 2-h OGTT ≥ 11.1 mmol/L.

14

Treatment and prognosis

Education first, metformin next, insulin always in type 1.

Everyone

Education and self-monitoring

Treatment depends on symptoms and how high the sugars are. Everyone sees a diabetes educator / dietitian; learns to check their own blood sugar (glucometer + finger prick); registers with the NDSS (National Diabetes Services Scheme) for free insulin needles and discounted strips.

Diet

Diet-controlled diabetes

Not significantly different from healthy eating. Insulin users need regular meal times; overweight patients need calorie restriction. Prefer low-GI foods (large starch particles digest slowly). Limit salt and saturated fat — diabetes is an atherosclerosis risk factor.

Glycaemic index

The area under the plasma glucose curve for a given amount of carbohydrate ingested. Soluble, easily digested sugars have a high GI.

Metformin — the first-line oral drug

How it works↓ hepatic glucose production · ↓ intestinal glucose absorption · ↑ insulin-mediated glucose uptake
AdvantagesDoes not cause hypoglycaemia · no weight gain · does not depend on functioning β cells
When not first lineRenal impairment, GI intolerance, or sugars too high

Type 1 prognosis

  • Now similar life expectancy to type 2.
  • Leading cause of death in both types: cardiovascular disease.
  • Always on insulin, always needs background insulin — when unwell they need more, not less. Skipping it can precipitate diabetic ketoacidosis.
  • May use a pump ± sensor (sensor reads interstitial glucose in real time or over 7 days; expensive).
Link to L8

Diabetes is a major atherosclerosis risk factor (endothelial injury from hyperglycaemia — step 1 of the L8 cascade), which is why CVD is the leading cause of death.

15

Diabetic emergencies

Ketoacidosis and hypoglycaemia — and telling them apart.

 Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)Hypoglycaemia
WhoPrimarily type 1Anyone on insulin (or insulin-releasing tablets)
MechanismNo insulin → cannot use glucose → body breaks down fat → ketones → acidosisBlood glucose < 4 mmol/L or low enough to cause symptoms
OnsetProlonged (hours–days)Rapid, any time of day or night
FeaturesHyperglycaemia, polyuria, polydipsia, hyperventilation, dehydration; nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, acetone odourAdrenergic: pale, sweating, shaking, palpitations, anxiety. Neuroglycopenic: hunger, poor concentration, confusion, odd behaviour, coma, seizures
PrecipitantsInfection, insulin withdrawal (omitted doses common in young people), MI, traumaSkipped meal, too much insulin, exercise
TreatmentHospital: aggressive IV fluids + insulin; IV glucose once sugar falls; find the trigger15 g fast-acting glucose, then measure blood sugar
The DKA paradox

Hyperglycaemia corrects before the acidosis. Insulin must keep running to switch off ketone production, so IV glucose is given alongside it to stop the patient becoming hypoglycaemic while the pH recovers.

Hypoglycaemia unawareness

The absence of the usual warning symptoms as glucose falls. It raises the risk of severe hypoglycaemia and is more common in people with insulin-treated diabetes of more than 10 years. Ask about it before treatment.

From the lecture slides
16

Diabetes and the mouth

Periodontitis, saliva, caries, infection and healing.

Diabetes and periodontitis

Poorly controlled diabetes may be a risk factor for more severe periodontitis and poor response to periodontal treatment; consensus guidelines exist for dental and medical providers.

Does treating the gums improve diabetes?

A randomised trial of non-surgical periodontal therapy (scaling, root planing, chlorhexidine, supportive therapy at 3 and 6 months) in patients with type 2 diabetes was stopped early for futility: at 6 months periodontal health improved, but HbA1c did not differ from untreated controls. Earlier studies were mixed and smaller. So periodontal control does not necessarily lead to better diabetic control. The lecturer’s open question: does better diabetic control improve periodontal control?

The slide says “257 patients”. This is the DPTT trial (Engebretson et al., JAMA 2013), which randomised 514 participants — 257 to each arm.

Link to periodontology

In the 2017 periodontal classification, diabetes is a grade modifier: HbA1c ≥ 7.0% moves a patient to grade C (rapid progression).

Saliva, caries and infection

Salivary glands

Xerostomia and sialosis

Xerostomia is common (reason unclear); burning mouth syndrome (tender, painful, burning tongue); bilateral parotid enlargement (sialosis).

Caries

Increased caries

Xerostomia + increased salivary glucose; dysbiosis (altered environment and immunity); hyperglycaemia positively associated with caries.

Infection

Increased risk

Altered neutrophil and macrophage metabolism, inhibited phagocytosis; neuropathy and poor peripheral circulation; reduced antibody production. Candida infections are more common.

Healing

Delayed wound healing

Microvascular disease and impaired leucocyte function (L4).

T2DM comorbidities: non-alcoholic fatty liver diseaseHypertensionDyslipidaemia
List three oral manifestations of diabetes mellitus.

Any three of: more severe periodontitis with poorer treatment response; xerostomia; burning mouth; sialosis (parotid enlargement); increased caries; candidiasis and other infections; delayed wound healing. (Tutorial MCQ: of the options given, “increased Candida infections” is correct; salivary glucose is increased, not decreased.)

17

Dental appointments for diabetic patients

Prevention, recognition and the chair-side response.

Schedule in the morningNo skipped mealsGlucose source availableIs their diabetes well controlled?Do they have hypoglycaemic awareness?

Recognising the problem

Fast

Hypoglycaemia

Initial: mood change, decreased spontaneity, hunger, weakness; then sweating, incoherence, tachycardia; can progress to unconsciousness, hypotension, hypothermia, seizures, coma and death.

Slow

Severe hyperglycaemia

Prolonged onset. Ketoacidosis may develop with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and acetone odour.

If in doubt, treat as hypoglycaemia

The lecture notes it is often difficult to differentiate hypo- from hyperglycaemia. In practice, treat a symptomatic diabetic patient as hypoglycaemic: 15 g of glucose will rapidly reverse a hypo and does negligible harm in hyperglycaemia, whereas an untreated hypo can kill within minutes.

Managing a hypo in the chair

  1. Stop treatment
    Clear the mouth.
  2. Give 15 g of fast-acting glucose
    If conscious and able to swallow (glucose gel/tablets, juice or regular soft drink).
  3. Measure blood sugar
    Recheck after about 15 minutes and repeat if still low; follow with a longer-acting carbohydrate once recovered.
  4. If unconscious
    Nothing by mouth; call an ambulance; basic life support; glucagon by injection if available and trained.
  5. After treatment
    Attend to infection control and dietary intake.
A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c of 10% needs a molar extracted. What should you consider, what oral manifestation is linked to his diabetes, and which emergency worries you?

Considerations: an HbA1c of 10% means poorly controlled diabetes → higher risk of post-operative infection and delayed healing. Liaise with his GP about control and defer if the extraction is elective; take a medication history (insulin or sulfonylureas raise hypo risk; check for other comorbidities such as hypertension and renal disease); book a morning appointment; confirm he has eaten and taken his usual medication; check his blood glucose with a glucometer before starting; have glucose available; keep it atraumatic, and review healing.

Oral manifestation: e.g. severe periodontitis, candidiasis, xerostomia or delayed healing.

Emergency: hypoglycaemia (most likely to occur acutely in the chair, especially if he has skipped a meal or is on insulin/sulfonylurea). Severe hyperglycaemia/ketoacidosis develops slowly.

18

Summary and glossary

What to carry out of the lecture.

GI

Gut disease in the mouth

Coeliac → enamel defects, aphthae, glossitis. UC → pyostomatitis vegetans, aphthae. Crohn’s → cobblestoning, linear ulcers, tags, lip swelling, often before gut symptoms. OFG → Crohn’s-like granulomas without systemic disease; exclude CD, TB, sarcoidosis.

Endocrine

Diabetes

Hyperglycaemia from β-cell loss (T1) or resistance + β-cell failure (T2). Mostly asymptomatic; HbA1c ≥ 6.5%. Emergencies: hypo (fast, treat with 15 g glucose) and DKA (slow, hospital). Oral: perio, xerostomia, caries, Candida, slow healing.

Glossary

Villous atrophy
Flattening of small-bowel villi; the lesion of coeliac disease.
Skip lesions
Diseased segments separated by normal bowel (Crohn’s).
Transmural
Involving the full thickness of the bowel wall.
Non-caseating granuloma
Collection of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells without central necrosis.
Pyostomatitis vegetans
Pustular, “snail-track” oral lesions; a marker of IBD.
Faecal calprotectin
Neutrophil-derived stool protein; marker of bowel inflammation.
ASCA / p-ANCA
Serological markers favouring Crohn’s / ulcerative colitis respectively.
Orofacial granulomatosis
Orofacial granulomas without a recognised systemic condition.
Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome
Lip/facial swelling, recurrent facial palsy, fissured tongue.
Hormone
Substance carried in blood to act on distant target cells.
Feedback inhibition
Target-tissue activity suppressing the gland driving it.
Islets of Langerhans
Endocrine cell clusters of the pancreas (~1 million).
Insulin resistance
Reduced tissue response to insulin; core defect of type 2 DM.
HbA1c
Glycated haemoglobin; ~3-month average of blood glucose.
Glycaemic index
Area under the glucose curve after a set carbohydrate load.
DKA
Ketone-driven metabolic acidosis from insulin deficiency.
Hypoglycaemia
Blood glucose < 4 mmol/L or symptomatic low glucose.
Hypoglycaemia unawareness
Loss of warning symptoms as glucose falls.
Sialosis
Non-inflammatory bilateral salivary (parotid) enlargement.
Readings
